questions.enonce_markdown:
What role is played by each of the following in digestion?

(i) Salivary glands.

(ii) Oxyntic cells. *[13 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Salivary glands** *(4 marks)*

**Salivary glands** (parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands) secrete **saliva** through ducts into the mouth, in response to the sight, smell or taste of food and to chewing (a reflex controlled by the brain). Saliva:

1. **Moistens and lubricates** the food with **mucus (mucin)** and binds it into a ball (**bolus**), so it is swallowed easily.
2. **Dissolves** some of the food, so it can be tasted by the taste buds.
3. Contains **salivary amylase (ptyalin)**, which begins the digestion of **cooked starch to maltose** (optimum pH about 6.8 and activated by chloride ions).
4. Is slightly alkaline (hydrogencarbonate ions), which **keeps the mouth at a suitable pH** for amylase and neutralises acids that would damage the teeth.
5. Contains **lysozyme** (and other antibacterial substances) which kills bacteria and so protects the mouth and teeth.

**(ii) Oxyntic cells** *(9 marks)*

**Oxyntic cells** (also called **parietal cells**) are found in the **gastric glands** of the stomach wall (in the fundus and body region). They have many mitochondria and deep, folded canaliculi that give a large surface. They secrete **hydrochloric acid** and **intrinsic factor**.

**How the acid is made.** Inside the cell **carbonic anhydrase** catalyses $\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-}$. The $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are pumped into the stomach lumen by the **proton pump ($\mathrm{H^+/K^+}$-ATPase)** using ATP, and chloride ions follow through channels, so HCl is formed in the lumen (**pH 1 to 2**). The hydrogencarbonate ions leave into the blood in exchange for chloride.

**Roles of the hydrochloric acid**

1. It gives the **low pH (about 2)** which is the **optimum for pepsin**.
2. It **activates the inactive precursor pepsinogen** (secreted by the chief cells) into the enzyme **pepsin**, which then also activates more pepsinogen.
3. It **kills most bacteria** and other microorganisms that are swallowed with food, so protecting the body from infection.
4. It **denatures proteins** and softens connective tissue in meat, making them easier for pepsin to attack; it also helps to dissolve minerals.
5. It **stops the action of salivary amylase** (which needs a neutral pH) once food is mixed with the gastric juice.

**Intrinsic factor** is a glycoprotein that binds **vitamin B$_{12}$** so that it can be absorbed in the ileum; without it **pernicious anaemia** results, because red blood cells cannot mature.

**Control.** Secretion is stimulated by the sight and smell of food (vagus nerve) and by the hormone **gastrin**, released from the stomach wall when food enters the stomach.

questions.enonce_markdown: How is the structure of the ileum suited to its function of absorption? *[7 marks]* *(4, 9, 7 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **ileum** is the part of the small intestine where most digested food is absorbed. Its structure is adapted for absorption as follows:

1. It is **very long** (several metres in man), so food stays for a long time in contact with the absorbing surface.
2. Its inner wall is folded into millions of finger-like **villi**, and each epithelial cell has **microvilli (brush border)** on its free surface. These give a **very large surface area** for absorption.
3. The **epithelium is only one cell thick**, so the **diffusion distance** between the lumen and the blood is very short.
4. Each villus has a dense network of **blood capillaries** with thin walls. Absorbed glucose, amino acids, vitamins and minerals enter the blood, which carries them away to the hepatic portal vein. This keeps the **concentration gradient** steep.
5. Each villus has a **lacteal** (blind-ending lymph vessel) which absorbs the products of fat digestion (fatty acids and glycerol, re-formed into fat droplets) into the lymph.
6. The epithelial cells have **many mitochondria** to give the ATP needed for **active transport** (e.g. of glucose and amino acids, with sodium ions) so that all the food is absorbed even when its concentration in the lumen is low.
7. Thin **muscle fibres in the villi** contract and relax, moving the villi and mixing the contents; **peristalsis** and segmentation also move and mix the food, bringing fresh digested food against the wall.
8. **Goblet cells** secrete mucus that lubricates and protects the wall, and the **brush-border enzymes** (maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases) complete digestion right at the surface.

**Diagram expected.** Draw a labelled villus (longitudinal section): epithelium with microvilli, goblet cell, capillary network, lacteal, muscle fibres, and the crypt of Lieberkuhn at its base, with arrows showing the entry of glucose and amino acids into the capillary and fatty acids into the lacteal.
